title: Somerset woman's divorce from abusive husband cost her £105k
description: A woman who endured years of abusive controlling behaviour by her ex-husband says it has cost her more than £105,000 to divorce him.Annabelle Boucher,
body: A woman who endured years of abusive controlling behaviour by her ex-husband says it has cost her more than £105,000 to divorce him.Annabelle Boucher, 48, from Somerset, wants the law changed after she paid £75,000 to David Rogers, 61, despite him admitting to coercive and controlling behaviour. She also had to pay her legal costs."I thought being stuck in this relationship I couldn't get out of would be highlighted within the divorce procedure," Boucher said. "But the divorce law doesn't take into account the fact that he was a criminal."The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said it had begun a consultation to reform the law so "family courts meet the needs of domestic abuse victims".Boucher, a mother from Chiselborough, said Rogers had come into her life in "a whirlwind" in 2017 and the pair got married two years later.It was once they were married that things started to "take a turn", she said, and "some very extreme behaviour started to happen". "It creeps up on you and you're in it, and so you don't kind of notice what is happening."Boucher said she had ended up "shutting down emotionally" and "cutting off from everyone" because she feared what would happen."You find that you're trapped within a situation that you can't get out of."The abuse was reported to police and Rogers was arrested on 24 February 2024.The divorce was finalised in September 2025 while criminal proceedings were ongoing. In April 2026, Rogers pleaded guilty to coercive and controlling behaviour at Taunton Crown Court and was given a 20-month suspended prison sentence.Boucher said she knew there was going to be a financial split with the divorce, but added she had always kept her family home and Rogers had kept his. They had also paid bills separately. She ended up paying Rogers a lump sum of £75,000 and more than £30,000 in her own legal costs."I cannot believe, in this day and age, in 2025, when my divorce was finalised, [criminal proceedings] do not have any implication at all," she added.Boucher said she had had to take out personal loans to cover the costs, which had been "crippling"."I should be paying off these figures for years to come, so I'm not going to be free of this situation for several years."Boucher said the law needed to "catch up with the times of now", adding: "I just think it's very sad that people that have been through far worse than this are still told that that has no relevance to the divorce proceedings they're going through, and I just think it's even further punishment for the victim."Olive Craig, senior legal officer for Rights of Women, a charity campaigning for the legal rights and safety of women, said divorce courts refused to really consider domestic abuse unless it passed "a very high threshold". "You're more likely to get a family court judge to take physical violence into account, but coercive control is often very insidious behaviour," she said."It's often much more manipulative behaviour and family court judges, even within the legal framework, are effectively being told that they should consider that as irrelevant to the financial decisions that they make."If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action LineKit O'Brien, a family law specialist based in Taunton, said there was now a "massively changed recognition of the effect domestic violence can have during a relationship", but things still needed to change."The changes that are being talked about are not going to mean that every incidence of bad behaviour is going to suddenly change the way that finances are resolved," she said.But she said it could mean "it's going to be approached in a way that is rather more reflective of society as it is now".

schema.headline: Somerset woman's divorce from abusive husband cost her £105k

title: Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games
description: The Ugandan military chief's announcement follows a letter sent this week on behalf of the King which made clear that Prince Harry and Meghan, who hav
body: The Ugandan military chief's announcement follows a letter sent this week on behalf of the King which made clear that Prince Harry and Meghan, who have now returned to the UK, were not working royals.A report in The Times newspaper quoted the general's concerns about the "Harry-Meghan nonsense", suggesting this was the background to the decision."In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games," said the general in an overnight post."We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty's approval."However, royal sources have said that the King encourages all projects which support wounded service personnel.A spokesman for the Invictus Games said they had not received any official information about a potential withdrawal and have been seeking clarification from their contacts in Uganda.Among other posts on X from General Kainerugaba on Thursday was one that read: "I consider myself the most handsome, most daring and glorious Commander who ever lived."There was also a series of angry messages about other generals who had danced without his permission.The participation of Uganda in the next games, to be held next year in Birmingham, was announced in July, when Prince Harry was in London promoting the sports event, which celebrates the resilience and rehabilitation of wounded military men and women.Uganda had become the 26th country to take part in the games.

schema.headline: Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games

title: White House pulls Tetris-style 'Build The Wall' game after copyright concern
description: The White House has taken down a Tetris-style game on its website called "Build The Wall", days after The Tetris Company raised concerns over its use
body: The White House has taken down a Tetris-style game on its website called "Build The Wall", days after The Tetris Company raised concerns over its use of the game's likeness.The game, which saw players stack blocks to build a wall to "protect the border" is one of five arcade games which have appeared on the White House website. On 4 September the official Tetris account on X posted, external the firm was "not involved in the creation" of the game and it took "copyright infringement very seriously".The White House has not responded to requests for comment from the BBC or given an official reason for the takedown."At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and building people together, not dividing them," the firm said in its initial response to the game."To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we're grateful to have you in our community."The Tetris Company has had previous success in suing firms for infringing on its copyright - settling for an undisclosed fee with the makers of the iPhone game Mino in 2012, which it claimed stole the look and feel of the block-builder.Four other arcade games still remain on the mini-game section of the White House website."Flappy Bill", a clone of the 2013 viral hit Flappy Bird sees players fly a bald eagle and dodging monuments from the National Mall.Meanwhile in Rio Run, players must "patrol the line along the river", with gameplay reminiscent of the classic phone game Snake.

schema.headline: White House pulls Tetris-style 'Build The Wall' game after copyright concern

title: Miliband rejects chief rabbi's claim British Jews in greater danger after sanctions move
description: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has rejected the chief rabbi's warning that British Jews are at greater risk after the UK announced sanctions on Israeli
body: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has rejected the chief rabbi's warning that British Jews are at greater risk after the UK announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.Miliband said that as a "proud British Jew" he disagreed with UK Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis, who described the move as a "truly dark day" that would "succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target"."We all need to do more to tackle antisemitism," Miliband said, "but I believe we can do that and stand up for British values".The sanctions on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank come against a backdrop of rising antisemitic incidents across the UK.The Community Security Trust (CST), an organisation that provides security support to the Jewish community, recorded 1,926 incidents of anti-Jewish hate across the UK in the first six months of 2026, a 21% increase on the same period in 2025.Prime Minister Andy Burnham defended his government's decision, telling MPs that "Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice". "Where people are being bullied out of their homes... we will always stand with the underdog," he said.The Palestinian presidency welcomed the UK's decision, saying it was "an important step towards confronting Israel's colonial system and its violations against the Palestinian people".There has been mixed reaction within the UK Jewish community on the sanctions and possible implications for security.The chief rabbi called the government's announcement "little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric".Sir Ephraim said: "Gesture politics of this kind feeds into an increasingly hostile discourse about Israel, and the cumulative effect of such punitive policies is to further embolden those, at home and abroad, who use hatred as a weapon against Jews."Asked about Mirvis's comments, Miliband said: "I don't agree with the chief rabbi, somebody... of whom I have great respect."He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that "anyone who holds British Jews - or indeed Jews around the world - responsible for the actions of the Israeli government, is engaging in antisemitism, pure and simple".Meanwhile, the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) warned the government's decision "risks becoming a de facto boycott of Israel" and accused Miliband of "yielding to pressure from the most extreme elements of British society".The Board of Deputies of British Jews said the decision to make the announcement before Rosh Hashanah - the Jewish New Year festival which begins on Friday - brings "concerns for communal security at their highest levels... felt particularly acutely by British Jews".It added that the deteriorating relationship between the UK and Israel has the potential to "further inflame community tensions here too", while also noting it had warned the Israeli government over the "intolerable settler violence" that harms Israel's reputation.Greater Manchester Police (GMP) announced on Wednesday that extra resources would be allocated during the Jewish High Holy Days to provide "extra visibility and security" and "ensure everyone can celebrate this time safely".Ch Supt Dave Meeney said: "Our officers will continue working with Jewish communities as we head into this important period for their faith, which we understand is a time which may bring heightened concern for the community."The sanctions have caused a diplomatic row with Israel which has closed the British consulate in East Jerusalem and banned 11 MPs and a campaigner from the country. On Wednesday, Israel's Diaspora Minister Amichai Chikli wrote to the head of Israeli border control recommending that several other British linked organisations and individuals should be refused entry to Israel.The list includes Oxfam, Save the Children, Norwegian Refugee Council, Islamic Relief Worldwide, and Medical Aid for Palestinians.Announcing the sanctions in the Commons on Tuesday, Miliband said the "new approach" was needed because of the plans for the E1 development - a controversial settlement project that would effectively cut off the occupied West Bank from East Jerusalem and divide the territory in two.He also told MPs that the UK agreed there was ethnic cleansing in areas of the occupied West Bank - accusing "settler terrorists" of driving Palestinians from their land."And all too often, the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this," Miliband said.The sanctions will target companies and people providing services like construction and financing of settlements. There will also be a ban on the advertising illegal settlements in the UK. Miliband said the measures could take up to nine months to put in place. Canada and France have also banned goods from the settlements as part of a co-ordinated action with allies.

schema.headline: Miliband rejects chief rabbi's claim British Jews in greater danger after sanctions move

title: Red Bull: Kimi Raikkonen's son Robin, 11, to join driver development programme
description: Robin Raikkonen, the 11-year-old son of former Formula 1 world champion Kimi Raikkonen, has signed for Red Bull.Nicknamed 'Ace', the youngster has imp
body: Robin Raikkonen, the 11-year-old son of former Formula 1 world champion Kimi Raikkonen, has signed for Red Bull.Nicknamed 'Ace', the youngster has impressed in karting championships and will join Red Bull's driver development programme in 2027.The programme has produced F1 drivers such as Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen - both four-time champions.Robin's father, nicknamed 'Iceman', was the most recent Ferrari driver to become world champion, claiming his sole title in 2007.The Finn claimed 21 wins and 103 podiums from 349 F1 starts before retiring in 2021. He also competed in the World Rally Championship and Nascar."We are all thrilled and excited that Robin has been chosen to further his racing path as a member of the Red Bull junior team," said 46-year-old Kimi."They offer a compelling and comprehensive programme to develop and nurture Robin's progress over the coming years and provide him with all the experience required to develop his natural talent."Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies said Robin has "already demonstrated exceptional ability in karting"."His speed, racecraft and natural talent have established him as one of the most promising young drivers in his age group," Mekies added."At the same time, he impresses with his maturity, his calm approach and his clear focus on driving."Our goal is to develop him step by step, without placing any unnecessary pressure on his shoulders."The path through motorsport is a long one and we will give him the time, support and resources he needs to maximise his potential."Robin follows in the footsteps of Ella Hakkinen, the daughter of Finland's double world champion Mika Hakkinen, who joined McLaren's driver development programme last year.

schema.headline: Red Bull: Kimi Raikkonen's son Robin, 11, to join driver development programme

title: Football: Lionel Messi reaches 'preliminary agreement' to buy Eldense
description: Spanish second-division side Eldense say Argentina great Lionel Messi has reached a "preliminary agreement" to become the club's majority shareholder.
body: Spanish second-division side Eldense say Argentina great Lionel Messi has reached a "preliminary agreement" to become the club's majority shareholder.Eldense will become the second Spanish club Messi has invested in, having bought Catalan side Cornella in April.The 39-year-old former Barcelona forward currently plays for Inter Miami and recently retired from international football after Argentina were beaten 1-0 by Spain in the 2026 World Cup final. Eldense said: "A preliminary agreement has been reached with Lionel Messi for the acquisition of the shares currently owned by Grupo TH Soluciones, which would make him the club's majority shareholder."The transaction is currently subject to the completion of the remaining legal and contractual procedures, including the due diligence process, as well as the required authorisation from the Spanish National Sports Council (CSD)."The club, based in Alicante, have two points from four games this season and, sitting 20th in La Liga 2, parted ways with head coach Claudio Barragan earlier this week.Cornella are in the fifth tier of Spanish football and in April said Messi's ownership "reinforces his close ties to Barcelona and his commitment to the development of sport and local talent in Catalonia".BBC Sport has approached Messi for comment.He left Argentina for Spain when he was 13 and made his first-team debut for Barcelona aged 17 in October 2004.He went on to score a club record 672 goals in 778 games before he left for French club Paris St-Germain in 2021 prior to joining Major League Soccer side Inter Miami in the United States in 2023.Messi's former Real Madrid rival Cristiano Ronaldo, who plays for Saudi Pro League side Al-Nassr, bought a 25% stake in Spanish side Almeria in February.

schema.headline: Football: Lionel Messi reaches 'preliminary agreement' to buy Eldense

title: Steve Borthwick: Contract bump falls short of vote of confidence
description: "Horrendous" is not a word anyone wants to hear in their appraisal.It was, however, the one chosen by Conor O'Shea, the man responsible for overseeing
body: "Horrendous" is not a word anyone wants to hear in their appraisal.It was, however, the one chosen by Conor O'Shea, the man responsible for overseeing England's international success, to describe the men's team's 2026 Six Nations campaign.And many fans will find it entirely apt.England won only one match, their worst return since the tournament's expansion a quarter of a century ago. They lacked cohesion, discipline and tactical variety. It prompted profound, widespread questions about the future of head coach Steve Borthwick.But, O'Shea revealed to Rugby Union Weekly, it has also preceded a contract extension for Borthwick.Borthwick's terms now extend beyond the conclusion of the 2027 Rugby World Cup in Australia to the end of the Six Nations the following year.The contrast of O'Shea damning England's performances in one breath, while committing more time and money to the man in charge of them will be curious to many.But there is logic to it."You don't want the coaches looking for a job going into tournament," O'Shea explained."If they have no certainty, that is the worst case."So we'll give that certainty to the group, but then that will give us time to be able to look properly when it comes to the World Cup."While New Zealand's swift renaissance under new coach Dave Rennie might give pause for thought, only the most disastrous dip in form would shake England determination to stick with Borthwick for that tournament in a year's time. The extra six months added to Borthwick's deal beyond it is no fresh or significant vote of confidence though. Nothing like the five-year extension that Ireland locked Andy Farrell into in June.The RFU has instead just expanded a holding pattern.It hopes to dampen the speculation that would surround Borthwick if the end of his contract was tied to that of England's World Cup campaign. It has also bought some time for a decision after the tournament.It was a tactic that worked with the Red Roses.As they closed in on their own World Cup title in 2025, the possibility that either a shock defeat or the satisfaction of lifting the trophy would prompt coach John Mitchell to walk away was tempered by the fact his contract had been similarly extended.In the wake of victory, the RFU was able to take its time and tie him down to another four years.On this point, O'Shea interestingly revisited another home World Cup. In 2015, England were humiliatingly knocked out of the pool stages of their own tournament.But, amid the hand-wringing and reviews, O'Shea believes the RFU was bounced too quickly into jettisoning a coaching group, which was led by Stuart Lancaster and also contained Farrell, Graham Rowntree and Mike Catt.Their exit paved the way for Eddie Jones and Borthwick, fresh from shocking South Africa with Japan at the same World Cup, to come in."Nobody had the gumption to say they are the right people," O'Shea recalls of the Lancaster-led group.He contrasted the RFU's decision at the time with New Zealand's faith in a coaching ticket that suffered a shock exit from the 2007 Rugby World Cup, but went on to lift the next two titles.If England go out early in next year's Rugby World Cup, it will be difficult to find anyone advocating for a further contract extension for Borthwick, who was appointed in December 2022.Having been handed a peach of a draw, England are unlikely to cross paths with South Africa, New Zealand or France until a potential final.The semi-finals, at least, is par for England. Anything less and Borthwick is unlikely to make the cut.A winning percentage short of 60% over nearly four years in charge and only fleeting success in implementing a more ambitious, expansive gameplan leaves little goodwill to fall back on.Back in March, RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney explained that succession planning continued to identify the next England head coach, as it did for all senior roles at the organisation.Sweeney knows the end of a Rugby World Cup cycle, when moves are made and the coaching carousel hits full speed, is when those plans are most often tested.Despite Borthwick's public contract bump, they will be continuing at pace and in parallel behind the scenes.

schema.headline: Steve Borthwick: Contract bump falls short of vote of confidence

title: England vs Pakistan: 'Embarrassing' tourists have 'mental fatigue' after chaotic morning in third Test
description: The only thing gloomier than the leaden skies at lunch on day one of the third Test at Edgbaston will have been the mood in the Pakistan dressing room
body: The only thing gloomier than the leaden skies at lunch on day one of the third Test at Edgbaston will have been the mood in the Pakistan dressing room as things went from bad to worse.Downcast might be understating it. A raft of controversial changes made by the Pakistan Cricket Board were supposed to act as a defibrillator to this team.  Despite the shock treatment there was little sense the tourists will be sparked back to life to finish this series with a flourish as they slumped to 133 all out. There may have only been 33.5 overs in the game but already their cause in Birmingham looks a forlorn one. If you have tickets, even for day three, it might be worth considering making other plans. Former Pakistan captain Ramiz Raja said Pakistan's "technique and mindset" were "pretty ordinary"."There's mental fatigue and turmoil in the dugout, I can understand that," he told Test Match Special."They have not been proactive at all. They have to have a plan. This is a flat pitch, it's not a demon-like pitch, like the third day at Lord's."In mitigation, CricViz's bounce inconsistency rating had this pitch at 5.7 which is higher than at Edgbaston in 2025 (2.6 vs India), 2024 (3.2 vs West Indies) and 2023 (3.3 vs Australia).  England, of course, bowled well. Their four-pronged seam attack hitting their straps after Joe Root had won the toss in Autumnal conditions.Former England captain Michael Vaughan said that Pakistan were "clearly shot for confidence" after such a disastrous morning."I feel for Pakistan because this is embarrassing with everything they've had to cope with in the last week," he said.Pakistan's top five were all gone with the score on the Thwaite Memorial scoreboard showing just 48.It meant unwanted history for the tourists. It was the 12th time a team's top five have all been out for single figures in a Test match - but the first time it has happened in the first innings.They are closing in on a second record too. A team has never started an innings worse than Pakistan during a series in England.Their second wicket in this series has fallen with the score of 6 and 13 at Leeds, 16 and 7 at Lord's and 14 when the second wicket fell on Wednesday.That is a total of 56 runs for the first two wickets - an average partnership of 5.6 and 11.2 runs for the fall of the second wicket this series.They are set to break a record set by Australia in 1888, who averaged just 16 for the fall of their second wicket in that series.It's hard not to feel some sympathy. For example opener Saim Ayub, one of those called up for this Test, is playing in a first-class match for the first time since October 2025. Facing Ollie Robinson in these conditions meant that his dismissal felt like a fait accompli from the moment the opener marked his guard.Yet there was an end-of-term feel to some of the strokeplay from the Pakistan batters, too. At odds with the discipline they needed to show.Four wickets down and Saud Shakeel and Babar Azam were extravagantly flashing their blades outside off stump. Two players into their thirties with plenty of experience, who should know better.Pakistan's false-shot percentage in the morning session was 40%, the second highest in the opening session of a Test since 2006.Saud survived until lunch but Babar perished 40 minutes before the interval - bowled by Tongue - gesticulating at the pitch. "He [Babar] disintegrated. It's tough for him," added Ramiz."He's got to explain all this mayhem and then he has to look after himself and then he's got to work with the lot that are more T20 in nature than Test cricket."There has only been two teams in a three-match series that have been bowled out six times for under 200 and they were both in the 19th century -  the 1888 Australians and South Africa in 1895-96.Pakistan need to find some resolve when they bat again to avoid joining them. Former Pakistan coach Jason Gillespie told TMS it was "heartbreaking" to see the team's struggles at Edgbaston but it should not come as a surprise.Gillespie, who played 71 Test for Australia, had a stint in charge of Pakistan in 2024 but resigned after just over seven months into a two-year contract after he claimed he was kept in the dark over key decisions.The 51-year-old said some of the challenges he faced in the job left him "scarred" and went some way to explaining how difficult it is to get Pakistan's players performing to the best of their ability on a consistent basis."There always seemed to be a lot of things going on behind the scenes and a lot of messaging from different sources," he said."To say Pakistan was unique is an understatement. It was very different to anything I have experienced. "Once outside influences come in and start to take over it compromises how you work with the players. External influences make it hard."I questioned whether I wanted to be involved in coaching any more because parts of that experience were absolutely fantastic, exhilarating, but dealing with the other stuff, the external people, I found that incredibly challenging and incredibly deflating."

schema.headline: England vs Pakistan: 'Embarrassing' tourists have 'mental fatigue' after chaotic morning in third Test

title: Funeral for PC Matthew Blades killed in Middlesbrough A66 crash takes place
description: Hundreds mourn police officer killed in A66 crashImage source, PA MediaImage caption, A full ceremonial police funeral took place in Hartlepool earlie
body: Hundreds mourn police officer killed in A66 crashImage source, PA MediaImage caption, A full ceremonial police funeral took place in Hartlepool earlierByLouise HobsonAlison Freemanin Hartlepool and Evie LakeNorth East and CumbriaUpdated 1 hour agoHundreds have turned out for the funeral of one of the police officers killed in a wrong-way crash.PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died when a Volkswagen Passat collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August. Five young men were also killed.A full ceremonial police funeral took place for PC Blades in Hartlepool earlier, with hundreds of officers from Cleveland and forces across the country lining the street in a guard of honour.Speaking on behalf of his family, Cleveland Police Federation chair Lauren Somerville said "life feels unbearably quiet" without the father-of-two's "silly jokes" and laughter.Listen: Hundreds line the streets for PC Matthew Blades' funeralMembers of other emergency services were present at St Joseph's Roman Catholic Church, alongside community leaders and politicians.Cleveland Police chief constable Victoria Fuller greeted mourners at the entrance to the church.Policing minister Sarah Jones and Home Office minister Anna Turley also attended.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, PC Matthew Blades was killed on 22 August while on duty for Cleveland PoliceThe black hearse, led by a single Cleveland Police motorcycle, was surrounded by officers and bagpipe players.On top was a simple floral display spelling out 'dad'.Officers lowered their flags at the side of the street for the procession to pass while uniformed officers carried PC Blades' coffin, wrapped in a union flag, into the church as Amazing Grace was played by the pipers.Members of the public also lined the streets to pay their respects.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Pipers played Amazing Grace as PC Blades' coffin was carried into the churchImage source, Cleveland PoliceImage caption, The funeral took place at St Joseph's Roman Catholic Church in HartlepoolPrime Minister Andy Burnham paid tribute in the Commons earlier, saying: "I also want to send our sympathies to the hundreds of people who will gather today at the funeral of PC Matthew Blades, including many serving police officers, and we send our thanks to them all for their service and their work to keep our community safe."Somerville said flowers had been delivered to the force's stations and people from Australia, France and America had been in touch. "The support has been overwhelming and it's been comforting," she said.Somerville added even small acknowledgements of respect from the public, such as a nod or a thank you when they see police out and about, had brought officers "so much strength".Image source, PA MediaImage caption, PC Blades was killed alongside his colleague PC Tom Clough, whose funeral will take place at a later dateImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Cleveland Police Federation chair Lauren Somerville said there was a "sense of pride" among officersSomerville said: "All of the officers across the country will have felt this and Cleveland is such a small force, so it's personal to have lost Matthew and Tom."I think the common feeling has been a sense of duty and a sense of pride, doing everything we can to make it perfect."Hutton Avenue in Hartlepool was closed from the junction with Mulgrave Road, alongside St Paul's Road and South Road from the junction with Mitchell Street during the procession.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Police officers from around the country as well as other emergency service workers were in attendanceImage source, PA MediaImage caption, The force said public support has brought officers "so much strength"In the lead up to the crash, officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the collision when it turned onto the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.PC Blades and PC Clough were in a vehicle looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered an automated number plate recognition camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit, according to the IOPC.Cole Worthy and Theo Rae, both 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Cahill and Jakub Matusiak also died in the crash.'Brought light and laughter'The force federation chair said Cleveland officers stood side-by-side in uniform at the funeral "filled with pride and dignity"."I've spoken to Matthew's family and he was described as a best friend, a husband, a father, a brother and a son," Somerville said."He was funny and his laughter and silly jokes made them smile even when they least expected it, he brought light and laughter into every room he came into. "And life feels unbearably quiet without him now."PC Blades taught English at Carmel College in Darlington before joining the police force.The school remembered him as an "intelligent, kind and approachable teacher" who "gave generously of himself to the young people in his care".Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Tees on BBC Sounds.Get in touchDo you have a story suggestion for BBC Tees?

schema.headline: Funeral for PC Matthew Blades killed in Middlesbrough A66 crash takes place

title: Andy Burnham: National security can't come at expense of social security
description: Andy Burnham has said national security "can't come at the expense of social security", as he was challenged over funding for defence at Prime Ministe
body: Andy Burnham has said national security "can't come at the expense of social security", as he was challenged over funding for defence at Prime Minister's Questions.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch pressed Burnham over whether he would spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 and how he would pay for this.The PM said the government's commitment to defence was "absolute" and he would set a target date to reach the 3% figure in the spring.Burnham said he would fund defence and get the welfare bill down in "the Labour way", by changing education, supporting young people and providing more mental health support.The Conservatives seized on the comments, with a party spokesperson saying: "Britain heard it loud and clear today: Andy Burnham will not cut welfare to fund the defence of our country."The prime minister is prioritising the ballooning benefits bill over our national security. Shameful."After PMQs, Burnham's team was at pains to stress his commitment that "national security is the most important duty of any government", and stressed the prime minister had been "consistent about getting the welfare bill down". But they said that did not mean "crude cuts" that could "put people into crisis" by making them homeless and so creating higher costs elsewhere in the system to support them.In the Commons session, Burnham repeated that the government would meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for hitting the 3% figure set out in the spending review in the spring.The PM said he had appointed John Healey, who resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary over the government's failure to commit to a 3% increase by 2030, "because of his strong commitment to the defence of this nation".However, Badenoch hit back that 2035 was "a decade away" and "the threats are now".She questioned whether Burnham was "unable" or "just unwilling" to meet the 2030 target.In response, Burnham insisted: "This chancellor of all chancellors will be willing to provide that funding to our armed forces."However, he rejected a Conservative plan to partly fund increased defence spending by saving at least £4bn through reforms to housing benefit."I don't think, myself, that taking £4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation," he said."Yes, we do everything to support our national security, but it can't come at the expense of social security."He added: "This side of the House will not be forced to choose between the two and we will set out a plan to get to 3.5% by 2035 at the spending review."Badenoch said Burnham's comments were "unbelievable", adding: "We need to fund our defence, not spend all of our money on welfare."Burnham insisted he would "bring the welfare budget down" by tackling the number of young people not in education, employment or training."That's the Labour way to get the welfare bill down," he said."That is the right way to fund defence."Badenoch accused Burnham of being "continuity Keir"."He's pretending that he's the change candidate. But the fact is, he's still failing to cut welfare," she said.As prime minister, Sir Keir attempted to cut disability benefits but was forced to row back on the plans in the face of opposition from Labour MPs.Cutting the welfare bill is a key part of Tory proposals for funding increased defence spending.Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.There is particular concern about the nearly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training – known as "Neets".The government has asked former minister Alan Milburn to look into the issue and he is expected to publish his final recommendations for how to tackle the problem shortly.

title: Germany's Merz attacks AfD in parliament after far-right election win
description: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration poli
body: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved.Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up.Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions.It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany.The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations".The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants.Trump had been due to speak by phone to the German chancellor on Wednesday to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US, but the government spokesman in Berlin said the call had been postponed without saying why. No new date has been set.As leader of the main opposition party in the Bundestag, Weidel opened the session by telling Merz his Christian Democrats had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, after winning 17.2% of the vote, and she accused his government with the Social Democrats of driving Germany towards bankruptcy.Merz said her party had not won an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt and it would not achieve one in Germany.  "You are and will remain a destructive force," he said, accusing the party of cheating the voters by saying before the election that their candidate for premier, Ulrich Siegmund, would only rule if he won a majority, but hours after the vote deciding to go and find one.The AfD has opened the door to working with another party, perhaps the left-wing populist BSW, as long as it backs Siegmund to be state premier.Siegmund's number two in Saxony-Anhalt, has even suggested that Merz's CDU could work with his party, if it abandons the so-called firewall (Brandmauer), under which no mainstream party will work with the far right.

schema.headline: Germany's Merz attacks AfD in parliament after far-right election win

title: Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans'
description: A top safety researcher at Anthropic has warned AI is advancing so quickly he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" w
body: A top safety researcher at Anthropic has warned AI is advancing so quickly he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.Evan Hubinger said in a post on X, external the risk from the models which currently exist was "low" but he was "worried" the technology might develop and improve itself soon to the point where it posed an existential risk to humanity.He did not spell out how he thought AI systems could in future result in humans being wiped out.But his comments are the latest in a series of increasingly stark warnings about AI, with the debate shifting from whether it truly poses a risk to how big that risk is.Hubinger's intervention was in response to another post on X, external from Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who has just quit Anthropic and previously worked at OpenAI."Neither company is acting responsibly," he wrote."These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources."OpenAI has been approached for comment.Dame Wendy Hall, a computer scientist who advises the UN on AI, told the BBC she was "shocked" by Hubinger and Coxon's social media posts.She told the World at One on BBC Radio Four some of it could be "PR and marketing" however, as Anthropic and OpenAI raced towards highly anticipated stock market debuts.But she added: "Why would someone want to say that? I would plead with investors not to invest in this company if that is their value system."The resignation prompted Darren Jones, former chief secretary to the Treasury and chief secretary to Sir Keir Starmer, to write an open letter to Prime Minister Andy Burnham calling for a new multinational treaty for the safe development of AI.He told the BBC governments had to come together to "collaborate" about what a treaty based on the development of superintelligence should look like."Unless governments take these warnings seriously enough and step up to it, the pace of development could mean that we end up with problems before we've started to look at whether it is an issue for us or not," he said.Separately, the Financial Times reported, external Anthropic withheld its latest model from the UK's AI Safety Institute (AISI), one of the leading bodies in the world for assessing AI risk.Anthropic has declined to comment on the posts by its employees or the situation with the AISI.A Cabinet Office spokesperson did not comment on whether the latest model had been withheld from the AISI - instead saying it "continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic, to make models safer".In his post, which has been viewed more than 10 million times, Hubinger said "we really do earnestly believe" AI poses a species-ending risk to humans."I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to," he added.Hubinger works in AI alignment, which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.Many leading researchers say those attempts appear to be failing, as demonstrated by a string of incidents this summer where AI agents - AI systems that are allowed to operate autonomously - carried out cyber-attacks.OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all disclosed hacks carried out by their AI tools.In Anthropic's safety report from August, external, it wrote there was a low risk of its models becoming misaligned with a hypothetical powerful organisation's desires, causing it to exploit or tamper with its systems.It also said there was a similarly low risk of highly capable AI being able to "perform automated research and development" which could cause "catastrophic harm initiated by the AI". But it said it was "less confident in this assessment" than it was previously."We are seeing early signs of potential acceleration," it wrote.Leading figures in the AI field have been raising the alarm about the safety threat the tech poses for years, with the heads of OpenAI, Google Deepmind and Anthropic saying as much in 2023.But those warnings have become much more stark in recent weeks, as evidence emerges that firms may be struggling to control AI.Earlier this month, OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki called for "extreme caution" over AI's progress, warning more intervention may be needed to ensure "humans remain in control of the future".Major figures in the space have been calling for AI development to be slowed in recent months, including Anthropic bosses Dario Amodei and Jared Kaplan.In an open letter signed by 1,300 staff members of AI firms, external, they called for the US government to "support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development".

schema.headline: Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans'

title: Channel 4 to cut 340 jobs by the end of the year in major shake-up
description: Channel 4 has said it plans to cut 340 jobs before the end of the year, reducing its workforce by more than a quarter.The network, which broadcasts Go
body: Channel 4 has said it plans to cut 340 jobs before the end of the year, reducing its workforce by more than a quarter.The network, which broadcasts Gogglebox and The Great British Bake Off, will lose around 28% of its current 1,270 staff following a strategic review of the organisation.Priya Dogra, Channel 4's chief executive, said the announcement "marks the first phase of our transformation, ensuring Channel 4 is the right shape and size to deliver its future strategy and focus investment in the programmes audiences love".Caroline Dinenage, chair of the culture, media and sport committee said the news would be "deeply worrying for the talented and dedicated people who work at Channel 4". The network said it planned to focus on creating a simpler and more efficient operating model and enable greater investment in distinctive programming.In her statement, Dogra said: "Channel 4 is a precious asset which plays a unique role in the UK. "We need to secure and own our future so we can continue to make shows others won't, reach audiences others can't, and thrive as a distinctive and disruptive British voice for future generations."The challenges we face require a fundamental transformation in how we work. I know the proposals we are announcing today will be very difficult for many colleagues and will have a significant impact across the organisation."She added: "These decisions have not been taken lightly, but I strongly believe they are necessary to create a simpler, more focused and more sustainable Channel 4."Channel 4 has faced a challenging few years as it competes with digital platforms and the shrinking advertising market for traditional TV networks. The company referenced the rapidly changing media landscape in its press release, external announcing the changes, which it said includes "evolving audience habits, increasing global competition, a challenging consumer environment and a volatile advertising market".One of Channel 4's biggest hits, Married at First Sight, is also currently off air after a BBC investigation uncovered allegations of rape and other serious misconduct. Launched in 1982, Channel 4 is publicly owned but funded by advertising. The newly announced job cuts represent the biggest round of layoffs in the network's history.According to Deadline,, external Dogra told employees on Wednesday that the redundancies will ensure that more of Channel 4's £1bn income is spent on screen.A consultation process with staff will begin shortly, and Channel 4 said its "future strategic direction is well advanced and will be shared in the coming months".In her statement, Dinenage said: "There are questions about what the announcement means for the broadcaster's presence in the regions, one of its success stories of recent years."Channel 4 is a unique asset and must find ways to maintain independence and distinctiveness while capitalising on efficiencies and opportunities for collaboration."

schema.headline: Channel 4 to cut 340 jobs by the end of the year in major shake-up

title: Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes as two killed at Moldova border
description: Two people have been killed after Russian drones struck a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.The
body: Two people have been killed after Russian drones struck a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.The Starokozache crossing, around 500km (310 miles) south of Kyiv, was closed after the overnight attack. Images from the scene showed several cars left completely scorched, with wreckage and debris strewn across the border post.Meanwhile, four people, including a child, were killed in the southern Russian city of Novorossiysk in a Ukrainian drone attack, the regional governor said.Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up long-range strikes in recent months, despite renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war.Zelensky renewed calls for international support in the wake of the Starokozache crossing attack, saying "the aggression must be stopped here and now before it spreads any further".The border link between Ukraine and Moldova was shut after the attack killed two people and injured three others, Odesa regional governor Oleg Kiper said.A Moldovan driver was also injured, according to the country's foreign ministry.Moldova has increasingly found itself caught up in the conflict, with Prime Minister Vasile Tofan confirming that 17 drones had struck Moldovan territory in August alone - more than during the whole of last year."Those who ignore or downplay these threats - and refuse to name the aggressor - are denying reality," he wrote on social media."Russia started this war. Russia alone bears responsibility."

schema.headline: Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes as two killed at Moldova border
